composition: The alloy is an Fe-based Fe-Mn-Al-C austenite-based duplex (triplex) composition. According to the classification scheme used in the review, austenite-based duplex low-density steels typically contain Al ~5–10 wt%, Mn ~5–30 wt% and C ~0.4–0.7 wt%, with balance Fe; the representative triplex composition of the SIP study is Fe-(26–28)Mn-(10–12)Al-(1.0–1.2)C. Specific alloys referenced for this class include Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.9C (SIP, Table 4), Fe-27Mn-11.5Al-0.95C, Fe-28Mn-12Al-1C and Fe-18Mn-9.6Al-0.65C (the latter with up to ~21% δ-ferrite). Al is the chief lightweighting element (a 1.3% density reduction per 1 wt% Al) but is also a strong ferrite stabiliser, so Mn and C are added as austenite stabilisers/formers to ensure that the austenitic phase forms the continuous matrix and is stabilised to room temperature; the relatively high overall alloying content gives this class a higher austenite stability than the ferrite-based duplex steels.
conclusions: Solution treatment at ~900–1100 °C plus water quenching produces the triplex γ + δ-ferrite microstructure with an austenitic continuous matrix containing 6–8% δ-ferrite stringers and intragranular nano-sized κ′-carbides/SROs. Because Al raises the SFE and SRO/κ′ produce glide-plane softening, twinning is suppressed and planar glide dominates; the uniformly arranged coherent nano-κ′-carbides sustain strain hardening (SIP), and in lower-C duplex compositions the austenite deforms by microband plasticity (MBIP). This class therefore reaches strength–ductility combinations comparable to second-generation AHSS / Mn-TWIP steels (e.g. Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.9C in the ST+WQ condition: UTS 875 MPa / TE 58%, Table 4), although its total elongation is lower than that of single-phase austenitic grades at similar strength (Fe-28Mn-12Al-1C with 8% δ: higher YS, TE 65%, versus TE 100% for single-γ Fe-28Mn-10Al-1C). The minor δ-ferrite transforms to brittle ordered B2/DO3, reducing ductility and toughness and increasing anisotropy, and the γ/δ interfaces are preferential crack sources; impact toughness of solution-treated/quenched Fe-Mn-Al-C steels is better than conventional AHSS but below austenitic stainless steels (a duplex Fe-18.1Mn-9.6Al-0.65C reaches 177.8 J/cm² at room temperature after 1000 °C/1 h). Overall, the austenite-based duplex/triplex Fe-Mn-Al-C steels are among the most promising lightweight grades because of their robust response to composition/processing variations and their superior strain hardening and energy absorption, though application properties (fatigue, formability, weldability) remain incompletely characterised.

aliases: γ+δ (triplex) in solution treated and water quenched condition

mechanisms: Process→microstructure: solution treatment in the single-austenite/two-phase field (~900–1100 °C) followed by water quenching (fast cooling) suppresses the formation of coarse intergranular κ-carbides that would otherwise develop during slow cooling or coiling, so the austenite matrix is retained with only fine decomposition products — short-range order below ~2 nm and possibly nano-sized κ′-carbides of 20–30 nm.

Phase-transformation mechanism: on cooling/quenching from solution treatment the high-temperature FCC austenite spinodally decomposes into solute-lean and solute-rich FCC austenite (γ′ + γ″); the solute-rich austenite orders to the L1₂ (SRO) structure, and further ordering of C into the octahedral interstitial site converts L1₂ into the perovskite-type E2₁ κ′-carbide (Fe,Mn)₃AlCx (x<1), which is coherent with the matrix (cube-on-cube, [100]κ//[100]γ, lattice misfit <3%).

Composition→phase constitution: Al is a strong ferrite stabiliser, so its high content introduces a disordered A2 to ordered B2 transition in the ferrite and raises the stacking fault energy (~110 mJ/m² for the SIP triplex alloy, ~80 mJ/m² for Fe-27Mn-11.5Al-0.95C); Mn and C as austenite stabilisers compensate for the ferrite-stabilising effect of Al, so the austenitic phase forms the continuous matrix and stabilises to room temperature alongside a small δ-ferrite fraction (typically 6–8%).

Microstructure→deformation: when the δ-ferrite content is below ~10%, plastic deformation is dominated by the austenite matrix, and the tensile response of the duplex/triplex steel resembles that of a fully austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steel, exhibiting an inflection in the strain-hardening rate.

SFE/SRO→planar glide: the high Al addition increases the SFE and suppresses deformation twinning, while the highly concentrated solutes and the SRO/nano-κ′ particles cause glide-plane softening; both effects localise slip into planar bands, so dislocation planar glide dominates regardless of the SFE and aging condition, with no dislocation-cell formation up to failure.

κ′-carbide→strain hardening (SIP): in the triplex steel, nano-sized κ′-carbides coherent with the austenite are uniformly arranged and sustain the strain hardening; the superior plasticity is attributed to homogeneous shear deformation of the austenite, i.e. shear band induced plasticity (SIP).

Austenite→MBIP (Fe-27Mn-11.5Al-0.95C): the austenite matrix deforms by massive slip bands and their intersections (microband induced plasticity, MBIP) with a work-hardening-rate inflection near 0.2 true strain, while the δ-ferrite accommodates less strain because it contains the ordered B2 phase.

δ-ferrite→brittleness: the δ-ferrite of high-Al duplex/triplex steels transforms to brittle ordered B2 and/or DO3, which reduces ductility and toughness and increases mechanical anisotropy; because of the deformation incompatibility between ferrite and austenite, the γ/δ interfaces act as the main crack sources.

Aging→properties: subsequent aging raises the yield strength by increasing the density of κ′-precipitates but lowers the strain-hardening rate (observed for the SIP triplex and Fe-28Mn-12Al-1C steels), so the ST+WQ single-austenite-with-SRO state combines high tensile strength with high ductility, whereas controlled cooling or short aging shifts the balance towards high yield strength with moderate ductility.

Strengthening balance: for this class, strength is provided by interstitial/substitutional solid-solution hardening (C contributes ~187–300 MPa/wt%; Al in austenite <10 MPa/wt%), grain refinement (Hall-Petch) and κ′-precipitation, while the austenite matrix supplies ductility and strain hardening through planar-glide-based mechanisms (MBIP/DSBR/SIP).
microstructure: The ST+WQ condition is a γ + δ-ferrite duplex (triplex) microstructure in which the austenite (γ, FCC) phase forms the continuous matrix and the δ-ferrite (BCC, which may transform to the ordered B2 and/or DO3 states) is present as a minor, thin strip-like/band-like constituent elongated parallel to the rolling direction (δ stringers). The δ-ferrite fraction is typically 6–8% for triplex steels — about 6% for Fe-27Mn-11.5Al-0.95C, ~8% for Fe-28Mn-12Al-1C, and up to ~21% for Fe-18Mn-9.6Al-0.65C. The austenite grain size is ~30–50 μm (about 30 μm for the SIP alloy of Table 4 and about 50 μm for Fe-27Mn-11.5Al-0.95C). Within the austenite grains, fine ordered structures are present: short-range order (SRO) <2 nm and/or intragranular nano-sized κ′-carbides (20–30 nm, e.g. the γ + 8% δ + κ′ (20–30 nm) as-quenched microstructure of the SIP alloy), which are homogeneously distributed and coherent with the matrix (lattice misfit <3%). The κ′ phase is the metastable (Fe,Mn)₃AlCx (x<1) with an ordered L′1₂ / perovskite-type E2₁ structure. In water-quenched Fe-(12–18)Mn-8Al-(0.4–0.8)C duplex steels, fine L′1₂ structures are observed in the austenite while B2 + DO3 domains develop in the ferrite. The high-temperature austenite thus decomposes during cooling into low-temperature austenite plus L1₂ (SRO) and, at high Al and C contents, into κ′-carbides even during water quenching.
processing: Process route (ST+WQ): the steel is solution treated in the single-austenite / two-phase region at ~900–1100 °C. Documented examples are Fe-27Mn-11.5Al-0.95C solution treated at 1050 °C and the Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.9C SIP alloy solution treated at 1050 °C for 25 min. Immediately after solution treatment the material is water quenched (fast cooling) to room temperature. Fast cooling/water quenching is used deliberately to avoid the formation of coarse intergranular κ-carbides and other coarse second phases; it leaves the austenite matrix with only fine-scale decomposition products (SROs <2 nm and possibly nano-sized κ′-carbides 20–30 nm). In the general processing scheme for austenite-based low-density steels, cold-rolled strip is solution treated at 900–1100 °C in the single-austenite field and then quenched in water (or oil or other media); an optional downstream aging treatment (commonly 500–700 °C for 5–20 h) is used only to develop precipitation hardening and is not part of the present ST+WQ condition. Prior processing in the broader route (laboratory scale) involves small ingots, homogenisation at 1100–1250 °C for 1–3 h and hot rolling to 2–5 mm at a finishing temperature of ~850–1000 °C, but the defining steps of this sample are solution treatment plus water quenching.
properties: Mechanical/characterisation behaviour specific to this class and its ST+WQ condition: the SIP triplex alloy Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.9C (water quenched from 1050 °C/25 min; γ + 8% δ + κ′ 20–30 nm; γ grain size ~30 μm; SFE 110 mJ/m²) gives UTS/TE = 875 MPa/58% at 10⁻⁴/s (Table 4). Fe-28Mn-12Al-1C (austenite-based duplex with 8% δ-ferrite, water quenched from 1050 °C/25 min) has a UTS similar to the single-phase Fe-28Mn-10Al-1C but a higher yield strength and a lower total elongation (65% versus 100% for Fe-28Mn-10Al-1C); the higher YS is attributed to nano-sized κ′-precipitates and the lower TE to the presence of the δ-phase and to κ′ strengthening. In the flow behaviour, the triplex steel in the ST+WQ condition shows a flow stress that increases almost linearly to high strains with an inflection in the work-hardening-rate curve analogous to TRIP/TWIP steels. For Fe-27Mn-11.5Al-0.95C (γ + 6% δ, γ grain size ~50 μm, SFE ~80 mJ/m², κ′ not detected by XRD) the work-hardening rate shows an inflection at a true strain of about 0.2. Impact toughness data (duplex Fe-18.1Mn-9.6Al-0.65C with 20–40% δ) reach 177.8 J/cm² at room temperature after solutionising at 1000 °C/1 h, comparable to duplex stainless steels; more generally the impact toughness of solution-treated and water-quenched Fe-Mn-Al-C steels is better than conventional AHSS but below that of austenitic Cr-Ni stainless steels. Characterisation techniques invoked for this class include optical microscopy (duplex γ + δ), X-ray diffraction (for κ′), TEM (ordered structures, SRO superlattice reflections) and secondary-electron/SEM imaging.
summary: The austenite-based duplex Fe-Mn-Al-C low-density steel (also called triplex steel) in the solution-treated and water-quenched (ST+WQ) condition. Its microstructure is a continuous γ-austenite matrix carrying a small amount of band-like δ-ferrite stringers together with intragranular nano-sized κ′-carbides and short-range order (SRO) domains. The material is solution treated in the ~900–1100 °C range and then water quenched, which suppresses the coarse intergranular κ-carbides that otherwise form on slow cooling/coiling. The central research question is how this high-Al, high-stacking-fault-energy austenitic matrix — with its SRO/nano-κ′ content and its minor δ-ferrite — controls the operative deformation mechanisms (planar glide, shear-band/microband plasticity) and the resulting strength–ductility behaviour.
unmapped: This sample denotes a generic austenite-based duplex (triplex) class; the review documents several specific alloys within it that differ in composition, δ-ferrite fraction and grain size — e.g. Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.9C (SIP, Table 4), Fe-27Mn-11.5Al-0.95C (MBIP, SFE ~80 mJ/m²), Fe-28Mn-12Al-1C (8% δ, SFE-based SIP example) and the leaner Fe-18Mn-9.6Al-0.65C duplex steel (up to ~21% δ).

The classification scheme places austenite-based duplex steels at Al ~5–10 wt%, Mn ~5–30 wt%, C ~0.4–0.7 wt% with a typical tensile window of UTS ~800–1300 MPa and TE ~10–40%, whereas the specific triplex/SIP example Fe-(26–28)Mn-(10–12)Al-(1.0–1.2)C sits at the higher-C end overlapping the fully austenitic class; this compositional spread should be kept in mind when comparing property values.
The review explicitly notes that fatigue behaviour, formability, weldability and coatability of Fe-Mn-Al-C steels, including this class, are not yet sufficiently documented to allow firm conclusions.
